subject: math
title: Money to $100: Coins, Bills, Making Change and Earning
seo_title: Grade 3 Money to $100 Math Worksheets (BC Curriculum, Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Financial literacy – fluency with coins and bills to 100 dollars, and earning and payment
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on money for the BC curriculum: name Canadian coins and bills, count money to $100, make amounts in different ways, make change by counting up, and solve earning and paying problems with cash or card. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Count money by value, not by the number of coins: biggest first, then count on. A quarter is 25¢.
key_sub: To make change, count up from the price: $2.75 → $2.80 → $3 → $5 is 5¢ + 20¢ + $2 = $2.25. Cash totals round to the nearest 5¢; card payments are exact.
body_html:
Canadian coins and bills

Know each coin by its value, not its size. The dime is the smallest coin, but it is worth more than the nickel. Canada has no pennies.

To make $1To make $2
4 quarters8 quarters or 1 toonie
10 dimes20 dimes
20 nickels2 loonies

Count money: biggest first

Sort the money from biggest to smallest. Count the dollars. Then count on the cents.

Example

Count 4 quarters and 3 dimes.

25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢. Then 110¢, 120¢, 130¢. 130¢ = $1.30.

Answer: $1.30

Make an amount in different ways

50¢ can be 2 quarters, or 5 dimes, or 1 quarter, 2 dimes and 1 nickel. For the fewest coins, use the biggest coin you can each time.

Make change by counting up

Start at the price. Count up to the next 10¢, then to the next dollar, then to the money paid. Add the jumps.

Example

A toque costs $12.50. Pay with a $20 bill. What is the change?

$12.50 + 50¢ = $13. $13 + $7 = $20. 50¢ + $7 = $7.50. Check: $12.50 + $7.50 = $20.

Answer: $7.50

Earning and paying

To earn money is to get money for work, like doing chores or selling lemonade. To pay, you can use cash (coins and bills) or a card (debit or credit).

There are no pennies, so a cash total is rounded to the nearest 5¢. A card payment is not rounded.

Total ends inCash roundingExample
1 or 2down to 0$3.42 → $3.40
3 or 4up to 5$3.43 → $3.45
6 or 7down to 5$3.47 → $3.45
8 or 9up to the next 10$3.48 → $3.50
0 or 5no change$3.45 stays $3.45

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
5 coins, so 5¢Count the value of each coin: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 65¢, 70¢
A quarter is 20¢A quarter is 25¢. Four quarters make $1
The nickel is bigger, so it is worth moreA dime (10¢) is worth more than a nickel (5¢)
4 quarters and 3 dimes is 30¢130¢ is $1.30. Do not lose the dollar
$5 − $2.75 = $3.25Count up: 5¢ + 20¢ + $2 = $2.25. One dollar was used to make the cents

faq.q: What money skills are in the BC Grade 3 math curriculum?
faq.a: Grade 3 financial literacy in BC is fluency with coins and bills to $100, and earning and payment. Students count Canadian coins and bills, make the same amount in different ways, make change and talk about how people earn and pay.

faq.q: How can I help my child count Canadian coins?
faq.a: Sort the coins from biggest value to smallest, then count on: by 25s for quarters, by 10s for dimes and by 5s for nickels. Remind them that the small dime is worth more than the bigger nickel, and a quarter is 25¢, not 20¢.

faq.q: Why are cash totals rounded to the nearest 5 cents in Canada?
faq.a: Canada stopped making pennies, so cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5¢: endings 1 and 2 round down, 3 and 4 round up to 5, 6 and 7 round down to 5, and 8 and 9 round up. Debit and credit card payments are charged the exact amount.

faq.q: What does “earning and payment” mean in Grade 3?
faq.a: Earning is getting money for work, such as doing chores or running a lemonade stand. Payment is how we pay for things, with cash (coins and bills) or with a debit or credit card.

sets.title: Coins and bills: names and values

items.q: What is the name of this coin?
items.e: This is the loonie. It is gold in colour, has 11 sides and is worth $1.

items.q: What is the name of this coin?
items.e: This is the toonie. It has a silver ring and a gold centre and is worth $2.

items.q: What is the name of this coin?
items.e: This is the quarter, worth 25¢. It is bigger than the nickel and the dime.

items.q: What is the name of this coin?
items.e: This is the dime, worth 10¢. It is the smallest coin, but it is worth more than the nickel.

items.q: What is the name of this coin?
items.e: This is the nickel, worth 5¢. It is bigger than the dime, but worth less.

items.q: How much is a quarter worth?
items.e: A quarter is worth 25¢, not 20¢. Four quarters make $1: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢.

items.q: How much is a toonie worth?
items.e: A toonie is worth $2. The loonie is the $1 coin. 2¢ and 20¢ are cents, but a toonie is two dollars.

items.q: The nickel is bigger than the dime. Which coin is worth more?
items.e: The dime is worth 10¢. The nickel is worth 5¢. The size of a coin does not tell you its value.

items.q: Which coin is worth the most?
items.e: Dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, loonie $1, toonie $2. The toonie is worth the most.

items.q: How many nickels make a quarter?
items.e: Count by 5s to 25: 5¢, 10¢, 15¢, 20¢, 25¢. That is 5 nickels. 4 nickels make only 20¢.

items.q: How many quarters make $1?
items.e: Count by 25s: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢. 100¢ = $1, so 4 quarters. 5 is right only if a quarter were 20¢.

items.q: How many dimes make $1?
items.e: $1 is 100¢. Count by 10s: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢ … 100¢. That is 10 dimes. 100 is the number of cents.

items.q: How many quarters make a toonie?
items.e: Four quarters make $1. A toonie is $2, so 4 + 4 = 8 quarters. 4 makes only $1. 10 is right only if a quarter were 20¢.

items.q: How many loonies make $5?
items.e: A loonie is $1. $1, $2, $3, $4, $5: 5 loonies. One $5 bill is worth the same.

items.q: How many $5 bills make $20?
items.e: Count by 5s: $5, $10, $15, $20. That is 4 bills. 15 comes from 20 − 5.

items.q: Which bill is worth the same as these two bills?
items.e: $10 + $10 = $20. So a $20 bill is worth the same.

items.q: How many $10 bills make $100?
items.e: Count by 10s: $10, $20, $30 … $100. That is 10 bills. 100 is the dollars, not the number of bills.

items.q: Which coins are worth the same as a quarter?
items.e: 10¢ + 10¢ + 5¢ = 25¢. So 2 dimes and 1 nickel make a quarter. 2 dimes make 20¢: that is the mistake “a quarter is 20¢.” 1 dime and 1 nickel make 15¢. 3 dimes make 30¢.

items.q: Jasleen says 3 quarters are worth more than 1 loonie because 3 coins are more than 1 coin. Is she right?
c: Yes. 3 coins are more than 1 coin.
No. They are worth the same.
items.e: 3 quarters: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢. A loonie is $1 = 100¢. 75¢ is less than 100¢. Count the value of the coins, not how many coins there are.

items.q: Put these bills in order from least to greatest.
items.e: $5 is the least, then $10, then $20, then $50: $5, $10, $20, $50.

items.q: How much money is shown?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 35¢, 40¢. That is 40¢. 5¢ counts the coins, not their value.

items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 80¢, 85¢. That is 85¢. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. 5¢ counts the coins, not their value.

items.q: What is the total?
items.e: Sort the money first, biggest value first. Start with the biggest coin and count on: 25¢, 35¢, 45¢, 55¢, 65¢, 70¢. That is 70¢. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. 6¢ counts the coins, not their value.

items.q: Hana brings this money to the school book fair. How much does she bring?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 85¢, 95¢. That is 95¢. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. 5¢ counts the coins, not their value.

items.q: How much money is shown?
items.e: Dollars: $1. Count on the cents: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢. $1 and 60¢ is $1.60. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. 4¢ counts the coins, not their value.

items.q: Kai has this money. How much does he have?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢, 110¢, 120¢, 130¢. 130¢ = $1.30. 30¢ forgets the dollar made by the cents. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. 7¢ counts the coins, not their value.

items.q: Lucas empties his piggy bank. How much money is in it?
items.e: Sort the money first, biggest value first. Dollars: $2. Count on the cents: 25¢, 30¢, 35¢. $2 and 35¢ is $2.35. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. 4¢ counts the coins, not their value. $1.35 counts a toonie as $1, but a toonie is $2.

items.e: Count the bills and dollar coins, biggest first: $2, $4, $5. Count on the cents: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢. $5 and 30¢ is $5.30. $6 counts every coin and bill as $1. $3.30 counts a toonie as $1, but a toonie is $2.

items.q: Arjun brings this money to the school book fair. How much does he bring?
items.e: Count the bills and dollar coins, biggest first: $5, $6, $7. Count on the cents: 25¢. $7 and 25¢ is $7.25. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. $4 counts every coin and bill as $1.

items.q: How much money is shown?
items.e: Sort the money first, biggest value first. Count the bills and dollar coins, biggest first: $5, $7. Count on the cents: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 85¢. $7 and 85¢ is $7.85. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. $6 counts every coin and bill as $1. $6.85 counts a toonie as $1, but a toonie is $2.

items.q: Owen has this money. How much does he have?

items.q: Zara empties her piggy bank. How much money is in it?
items.e: Count the bills and dollar coins, biggest first: $10, $15, $16, $17, $18. That is $18. $5 counts every coin and bill as $1.

items.q: What is the total?

items.q: Harjot brings this money to the school book fair. How much does he bring?

items.q: What is the total?

items.q: Ryan brings this money to the school book fair. How much does he bring?

items.q: Which money makes 40¢?
Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢, 50¢. That is 50¢. So two quarters is worth the same.

items.q: How many quarters make $2?
items.e: Four quarters make $1. $2 is 2 dollars, so 4 + 4 = 8 quarters. 10 is right only if a quarter were 20¢.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 60¢?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 25¢, 25¢, 10¢ = 60¢. That is 3 coins. 6 dimes also make 60¢, but that is more coins.

items.q: Which of these does not make 50¢?
items.e: 25¢, 10¢, 10¢ = 45¢, not 50¢. The others all make 50¢.

items.q: Which money makes $1.25?
Ethan has 3 coins. Together they make 45¢. Which coins does he have?
Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Count the bills and dollar coins, biggest first: $5, $10. That is $10. So one $10 bill is worth the same.

items.q: How many dimes make $1.50?
items.e: Ten dimes make $1. 50¢ is 5 more dimes. 10 + 5 = 15 dimes. 150 is the number of cents. 10 forgets the 50¢.

items.q: Which uses the fewest coins to make 75¢?
items.e: All of these make 75¢. 25¢, 25¢, 25¢ uses only 3 coins: start with the biggest one you can each time.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make $2.50?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: $2, 25¢, 25¢ = $2.50. That is 3 coins. A toonie is $2. Two quarters make 50¢. Loonies or dimes would take more coins.

items.q: Which money makes $12?
Which of these does not make $20?
items.e: $10, $5, $2, $2 = $19, not $20. The others all make $20.

items.q: Which uses the fewest bills and coins to make $15?
items.e: All of these make $15. $10, $5 uses only 2 pieces of money: start with the biggest one you can each time.

items.q: How many $10 bills make $60?
items.e: Count by 10s: $10, $20, $30, $40, $50, $60. That is 6 bills. 60 is the dollars, not the bills. 12 is the number of $5 bills.

items.q: Nadia has 3 bills. Together they make $35. Which bills does she have?
Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Count the bills and dollar coins, biggest first: $20, $40, $60, $80, $100. That is $100. So one $100 bill is worth the same.

items.q: Which of these does not make $5?
What is the smallest number of bills you can use to make $45?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: $20, $20, $5 = $45. That is 3 bills. $20 + $20 = $40, and $5 more is $45. Nine $5 bills take more bills.

items.q: Ava pays exactly $56 for a pair of soccer cleats. Which money could she use?
Jasleen buys a pencil for 40¢. She pays with a loonie. How much change does she get? Count up on the number line.
items.e: Count up from 40¢ to $1: 40¢ + 60¢ = $1. The change is 60¢. Check: 40¢ + 60¢ = $1. 40¢ is the price, not the change.

items.q: Chloe buys an apple for 65¢. She pays with a loonie. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count up from 65¢ to $1: 65¢ + 5¢ = 70¢, 70¢ + 30¢ = $1. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 30¢ = 35¢. The change is 35¢. Check: 65¢ + 35¢ = $1. 65¢ is the price, not the change.

items.q: Sofia buys a freezie for 85¢. She pays with a loonie. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count up from 85¢ to $1: 85¢ + 5¢ = 90¢, 90¢ + 10¢ = $1. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 10¢ = 15¢. The change is 15¢. Check: 85¢ + 15¢ = $1. 85¢ is the price, not the change.

items.q: Liam buys a granola bar for $1.45. He pays with a toonie. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count up from $1.45 to $2: $1.45 + 5¢ = $1.50, $1.50 + 50¢ = $2. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 50¢ = 55¢. The change is 55¢. Check: $1.45 + 55¢ = $2. $1.55 forgets that one dollar was used up to make the cents. $1.45 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Noah buys a bag of popcorn for $3.50. He pays with a $5 bill. How much change does he get? Count up on the number line.
items.e: Count up from $3.50 to $5: $3.50 + 50¢ = $4, $4 + $1 = $5. Add the jumps: 50¢ + $1 = $1.50. The change is $1.50. Check: $3.50 + $1.50 = $5. $2.50 forgets that one dollar was used up to make the cents. $3.50 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Hana buys a hot chocolate for $2.75. She pays with a $5 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count up from $2.75 to $5: $2.75 + 5¢ = $2.80, $2.80 + 20¢ = $3, $3 + $2 = $5. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 20¢ + $2 = $2.25. The change is $2.25. Check: $2.75 + $2.25 = $5. $3.25 forgets that one dollar was used up to make the cents. $2.75 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Wei buys a chapter book for $6. He pays with a $10 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count up from $6 to $10: $6 + $4 = $10. The change is $4. Check: $6 + $4 = $10. $5 counts the starting number as a jump. $6 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Kai buys a kite for $7.25. He pays with a $10 bill. How much change does he get? Count up on the number line.
items.e: Count up from $7.25 to $10: $7.25 + 5¢ = $7.30, $7.30 + 70¢ = $8, $8 + $2 = $10. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 70¢ + $2 = $2.75. The change is $2.75. Check: $7.25 + $2.75 = $10. $3.75 forgets that one dollar was used up to make the cents. $7.25 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Lucas buys a skipping rope for $4.80. He pays with a $10 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count up from $4.80 to $10: $4.80 + 20¢ = $5, $5 + $5 = $10. Add the jumps: 20¢ + $5 = $5.20. The change is $5.20. Check: $4.80 + $5.20 = $10. $6.20 forgets that one dollar was used up to make the cents. $4.80 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Emma buys a puzzle for $15. She pays with a $20 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count up from $15 to $20: $15 + $5 = $20. The change is $5. Check: $15 + $5 = $20. $6 counts the starting number as a jump. $15 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Arjun buys a toque for $12.50. He pays with a $20 bill. How much change does he get? Count up on the number line.
items.e: Count up from $12.50 to $20: $12.50 + 50¢ = $13, $13 + $7 = $20. Add the jumps: 50¢ + $7 = $7.50. The change is $7.50. Check: $12.50 + $7.50 = $20. $8.50 forgets that one dollar was used up to make the cents. $12.50 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Olivia buys a pair of swim goggles for $16.75. She pays with a $20 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count up from $16.75 to $20: $16.75 + 5¢ = $16.80, $16.80 + 20¢ = $17, $17 + $3 = $20. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 20¢ + $3 = $3.25. The change is $3.25. Check: $16.75 + $3.25 = $20. $4.25 forgets that one dollar was used up to make the cents. $16.75 is the price, not the change.

items.q: Owen buys a pair of shin pads for $35. He pays with a $50 bill. How much change does he get? Count up on the number line.

items.q: Mei buys a board game for $28.50. She pays with a $50 bill. How much change does she get?

items.q: Leah buys a scooter for $74.50. She pays with a $100 bill. How much change does she get?

items.q: Mateo buys an orange for 60¢ and pays with a loonie. Which coins could be the change?
c: a quarter, a dime and a nickel

sets.title: Earning and paying: chores, cash or card

items.q: Which of these is a way to earn money?
c: putting money in a piggy bank
items.e: To earn money is to get money for work. Doing chores for pay is earning. Buying and paying are spending. A piggy bank keeps money you already have.

items.q: Which of these can you use to pay at a store?
items.e: You can pay with cash (coins and bills) or with a card. A debit card takes the money from a bank account. A price tag shows the cost. A receipt shows what you paid.

items.q: Ryan earns $2 each time he walks the neighbour’s dog. He walks the dog 4 times. How much does he earn?
Ethan gets $5 each week for helping at home. How much does he get in 3 weeks?
items.e: Count by 5s: $5, $10, $15. That is $15. $8 comes from adding 5 + 3.

items.q: Nadia sells lemonade for 50¢ a cup. She sells 6 cups. How much money does she earn?
items.e: Two cups make $1. 6 cups is 3 pairs: $3. 30¢ counts each cup as 5¢. $2.50 is only 5 cups. $6 counts each cup as $1.

items.q: Ava does each chore on the chart once. How much does she earn?
items.e: 50¢ + 25¢ + $1 + 25¢: the two quarters make 50¢, and 50¢ + 50¢ = $1. $1 + $1 = $2. $1.90 counts a quarter as 20¢. 4¢ counts the chores, not the money.

items.q: Jasleen earns $10 for raking leaves and $7.50 for washing the car. How much does she earn in all?
items.e: $10 + $7 = $17. Add the 50¢: $17.50. $17 forgets the cents. $2.50 subtracts. $8.50 adds $1 instead of $10.

items.q: Chloe pays for this in cash. How much does she pay?
items.e: Canada has no pennies, so a cash total is rounded to the nearest 5¢. $4.98 ends in 8, so it rounds up to $5.

items.q: Sofia pays for this by debit card. How much does she pay?
items.e: Card payments are not rounded. Only cash is rounded to the nearest 5¢. She pays exactly $6.37.

items.q: Liam buys a bag of apples for $3.42. He pays in cash. How much does he pay?
items.e: Cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5¢. $3.42 ends in 2, so it rounds down to $3.40.

items.q: At a Kamloops farmers’ market, Noah’s total is $8.53. He pays in cash. How much does he pay?
items.e: Cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5¢. $8.53 ends in 3, so it rounds up to $8.55.

items.q: Hana wants a book set for $24. She has saved $15. How much more money does she need?
items.e: Count up: $15 + $5 = $20, $20 + $4 = $24. $5 + $4 = $9. $11 takes the smaller digit from the bigger one. $39 adds.

items.q: Wei saves $5 each week for a $30 lacrosse ball and net. How many weeks will it take?
items.e: Count by 5s to 30: $5, $10, $15, $20, $25, $30. That is 6 weeks. 25 comes from 30 − 5.

items.q: At the PNE in Vancouver, Kai buys a hot dog for $4.75 and a drink for $2.50. How much does he spend?
At a bakery in Victoria, Lucas buys a muffin for $2.85. He pays with a $5 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count up from $2.85 to $5: $2.85 + 5¢ = $2.90, $2.90 + 10¢ = $3, $3 + $2 = $5. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 10¢ + $2 = $2.15. The change is $2.15. $3.15 forgets the dollar used to make the cents.

items.q: Emma earns $12 at a family garage sale. She spends $7.50 on a book. How much money is left?
items.e: Count up from $7.50 to $12: $7.50 + 50¢ = $8, $8 + $4 = $12. Add the jumps: 50¢ + $4 = $4.50. $4.50 is left. $5.50 forgets the dollar used to make the cents. $19.50 adds.

items.q: For a field trip to Science World, each student brings $3 for the bus. 8 students bring their money. How much is that?
Arjun pays for a hockey stick that costs $34.50 with two $20 bills. How much change does he get?
items.e: Two $20 bills make $40. Count up from $34.50 to $40: $34.50 + 50¢ = $35, $35 + $5 = $40. Add the jumps: 50¢ + $5 = $5.50. The change is $5.50. $6.50 forgets the dollar used to make the cents. $14.50 uses one $20 bill only.

items.q: Olivia has 7 toonies and 3 loonies. Can she buy a $16 kite?
items.e: 7 toonies: $2, $4, $6, $8, $10, $12, $14. Add 3 loonies: $15, $16, $17. $17 is more than $16, so yes, with $1 left. “No, she needs $6 more” counts each toonie as $1.

items.q: Owen earns $3 each week for chores. He wants a $20 model kit. How many weeks until he has enough?
items.e: Count by 3s: $3, $6, $9, $12, $15, $18. After 6 weeks he has $18, not enough. After 7 weeks he has $21. So it takes 7 weeks. 17 comes from 20 − 3.
